| $150,000 converted into local currency | Benchmark for other countries, such as Australia (2022, older) | When judging purchasing power outside the US | L1092.034 |

- Use $100,000 as the general definition and the $100,000 to $400,000 band for the test. Use the roughly $150,000 US benchmark only as a purchasing-power reference that rises with inflation. [L0019.002, L1518.004, L0457.001, L1090.007, L1092.034]

### Price points and demographic fit

- Sofa examples: a roughly $200 cheap metal futon is typically bought by lower-income buyers. A roughly $1,500 average sofa fits the upper middle class, and a roughly $7,500 custom designer sofa is typically bought by wealthy buyers. [L1518.010]
- Alternative sofa values: a $200 futon, a $2,000 three-seater fabric sofa (realistic price, proportional expectations, fewer issues, strong profitability) and a $10,000 custom Italian leather sofa (high profit, intensive pre-selling, high return rate). [L0018.007, L1517.004]
- The $1,500 product or the $2,000 fabric sofa is the best fit for an upper middle class target, depending on which example set you use. [L1518.010, L1517.004]
- A high-priced product with a high margin, such as a $7,500 item at a 30% margin, is not automatically the best choice. Price must match the target demographic, because a product that appeals to the wrong buyers creates more service and return costs. [L1518.011]
- Do not choose a niche because a very expensive version looks attractive. A high-priced niche aimed at wealthy buyers can produce sales, but it brings heavy pre-selling and high return rates. [L1517.010]
- Chandeliers with an average search-term price of about $400 pass the test. For households earning $100,000 to $400,000, that amount is not a big decision. [L0457.005]
- For real crystal chandeliers, the first organic row averaged about $1,000, while later rows showed prices from about $4,000 up to over $450,000. Many of the most expensive listings were presumed to be real crystal pieces. [L0457.007]
- When organic listings show a very wide price spread for one search term, do not treat the whole range as one price point. Wide spreads often come from premium versions of the same product, so judge the typical buyer by the more mainstream listings. [L0457.017]
- An average price point around $10,000 to $20,000 generally means a wealthy demographic rather than upper middle class. Upper middle class households rarely spend at that level unless they are overextended on credit. [L0457.008]
- Futons with an average price above $200 can pass seasonality and demand checks but still fail the demographics test if their buyers are mostly first-apartment, dorm-room or parents' basement purchasers. [L0457.010]
- Stand-up desks pass by logic: lower-income households would not spend at that price point, and very wealthy buyers of custom pieces, such as a $15,000 mahogany desk, are not the core group. The core group is the upper middle class. [L0457.013]
- Stand-up paddleboards and paddles average over $700 in customer spend and appeal to upper-middle-class buyers seeking recreational products. [L0022.004]
- A very expensive outlier in a niche, priced far above the rest, can be listed for organic buyers. Keep it out of paid campaigns and off the ad budget, because it appeals to a different audience. [L0965.020]
- When a niche contains products across all price tiers and demographics, select one price tier that aligns with the target audience. Upper middle class customers are the most hands-off to serve. [L0278.020]
- Keep price tiers in separate stores when they serve different buyers, because a luxury buyer and a budget buyer shop differently. Put products in the same store only if they fit the same customer. (2020, older) [L1277.017]

### Demographic test

- The target demographic is the upper middle class, defined as households with an income of $100,000 to $400,000. A niche passes when its typical buyer falls in this income band. [L0457.001]
- The demographics test has no single data source or fixed score. It relies on judgement: estimate who actually buys the product at its price point and whether that buyer fits the upper middle class. [L0457.002]
- The demographics test is a separate filter that comes after the price point, seasonality and demand checks. A niche can pass all of those and still fail if its typical buyers are not upper middle class households. [L0457.016]
- Run the demographics test only on the current winners in your own niche list, not on rejected niches. Record the result in the demographic column of your Niche Research Worksheet. [L0457.015]

**Procedure: demographics test**

1. Check the average price of the niche search term. [L0457.003]
2. Ask whether a purchase at that price is a major financial decision for a household earning $100,000 to $400,000. [L0457.003]
3. If the price points sit in the wealthy range, or the buyers are mainly first-apartment, dorm or temporary buyers, consider pivoting sideways. [L0457.003]
4. If the niche still fails, look for a related sub-niche that fits the upper middle class. [L0457.003]

**Procedure: checking price points for a niche**

1. Search the niche term on Google. [L0457.006]
2. Open the Shopping results. [L0457.006]
3. Scroll down to the organic listings. [L0457.006]
4. Read the price of each listing. [L0457.006]
5. Compare the prices to estimate the average price point and the spread across listings. [L0457.006]

**Recording results**

- A green demographic box in the research tool means the niche passes the demographic test, meaning it appeals to the upper middle class. Record it as "pass" and do not write out the demographic label. [L1081.007]
- A green brand loyalty box means little to no brand loyalty, so the niche passes the brand loyalty test. Record it as "pass". [L1081.008]

### Cleaning the niche list

**Procedure: sorting the list against upper middle class criteria**

1. Open your research worksheet with your current niche list. [L1517.008]
2. Go through the list from the top and mark any niche that is too broad or covers a very wide price range. [L1517.008]
3. Copy the broad niche name and move it to the bottom of the list, so it is kept for reference but not researched further. [L1517.008]
4. Delete the original row of the broad niche. [L1517.008]
5. Ask an AI tool for sub-types of that niche that sell at a higher price point, for example at $500 or more. [L1517.008]
6. Insert each useful sub-niche as a new row, placed above the bottom reference section. [L1517.008]
7. Scan the rest of the list for niches that appeal to lower-income or wealthy buyers, and move them to the bottom. [L1517.008]
8. Replace low-price niches, such as futons, with higher-price alternatives in the same category, such as leather sofas, fabric sofas or sectional sofas. [L1517.008]
9. Keep niches you are unsure about on the list so they can be checked later with a demographic tool. [L1517.008, L1517.015]

**Procedure: refining niches in the research worksheet**

1. Open your Source A X Research Worksheet. [L0018.011]
2. Review each niche and assess whether it appeals to lower-income, upper-middle-class or wealthy demographics. [L0018.011]
3. Remove broad or ambiguous categories. [L0018.011]
4. Add niche variations that more clearly target upper middle class buyers. [L0018.011]
5. Use AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini or similar) to expand product variants using prompts like the one below. [L0018.011]
6. Keep any uncertain niches. The DSLX Software in Module 2 will automatically show which demographic each niche appeals to. [L0018.011]
7. Mark the lesson complete and move to the next one. [L0018.011]

Niches that are still unclear should stay on the list rather than be deleted, so they can be checked later with a demographic validation tool. Judging by intuition alone is acceptable at the early stage. [L1517.015]

### Pivoting broad niches

**Case: the rug niche**

- The niche "Rugs" was too broad. It included $30 to $500+ options appealing to all income levels. The niche was moved to the bottom of the research list without evaluation. [L0018.008]
- To refine it, the AI prompt "What type of rugs typically sell for $500 or more?" was used. It yielded upper-middle-class-targeted variations: woven rugs, oriental rugs and Persian rugs, which are naturally priced higher and more specific to the target demographic. [L0018.008]

**Prompt**

```
What type of [product category] typically sell for $500 or more?
```

[L0018.009]

- Replace broad niche categories with upper-middle-class-specific variations. For example, instead of "futons", use leather sofas, fabric sofas or sectional sofas, which appeal more strongly to the target demographic. [L0018.010]
- Pivot sideways or to a related sub-niche when a niche fails the demographics test. [L0457.003]
- Dropping an entire product does not always make sense. A product that is too narrow may be expanded or repositioned; see the Source C units in the audience section. [L0656.014, L0552.057]
- If a niche is dominated by a few big brands sold in large chains, choose a related sub-niche. Golf clubs from Titleist, Callaway, TaylorMade, Mizuno and Srixon are weak for this model, so choose sub-niches such as golf carts, electric golf trolleys or golf bags. [L0857.038]

### Brand loyalty: what it means

- A niche has brand loyalty when shoppers think of a few specific brands first when they want to buy a product in it, and those brands dominate the market. Avoid niches with brand loyalty for dropshipping. [L0455.001]
- Brand loyalty is a problem because established brands already occupy consumers' minds, leaving too few suppliers with enough sales potential to build a stable dropshipping business. The concern is the supplier side as much as the shopper side. [L0455.002]
- The Source A X methodology excludes niches with high brand loyalty, where shoppers strongly prefer specific brand names over product type. [L0021.001]
- High brand loyalty niches fail because approval from dominant brands is hard or impossible, and you cannot compete with major retailers such as Best Buy, Target or Costco. Big brands control distribution and attention, and competition is high while margins are low. [L0021.002]
- Strong niches have low brand loyalty: customers buy based on product type and features, multiple manufacturers compete evenly, and no single company spends hundreds of millions on advertising to control preference. [L0021.004]
- Select products where customers lack established brand loyalty. Customers in brand-loyal niches research extensively and default to trusted brands, which gives established retailers price and relationship advantages that dropshippers cannot match. [L0022.001]
- Choose products that meet all three criteria. Customers are comfortable buying from any manufacturer, they lack a default brand they automatically associate with the category, and no few manufacturers hold a monopoly. When these conditions exist, customers base decisions on price, reviews and personal preference rather than brand identity. [L0022.003]
- Target niches with low brand loyalty so new stores can compete. High brand loyalty niches require an established reputation and customer trust that new entrants cannot quickly overcome. [L0159.006]
- Target shoppers who have little to no brand loyalty and would be comfortable buying from any manufacturer. Shoppers should care about the product type, not the brand name on it. [L0988.002]
- Brand loyalty is one filter applied after the other niche criteria. A product should first pass the basic drop-shipping fit checks; only then does the brand loyalty check decide whether it stays on the list. [L0988.016]
- Customers will purchase from any manufacturer if the product is well represented online, the price matches their budget expectations and the product does not require a pre-existing brand preference. [L0319.007]
- Customers in non-branded categories often do not know which manufacturers produce what they buy. This absence of brand awareness is an advantage for e-commerce sellers, because buyers decide on design, price and features rather than loyalty. [L0319.018]
- Only sell products where customers have no established brand loyalty. [L0319.001]
- Brand presence alone does not rule out a niche. It matters only if the brand dominates the category so strongly that buyers think of it automatically. An established brand that merely exists in a category is not a reason to avoid it. (2019, older) [L0357.013]
- Avoid niches where buyers insist on one specific brand, such as tablets where buyers want an iPad. Niches where buyers choose by specifications such as size, color, voltage, material or number of components work well even when no brand is famous. [L0804.009] (2023)
- Choosing a product because you picture a particular brand when you imagine selling it is a warning sign. If your first thought is to sell a specific brand's product, the niche is probably brand-driven and should be avoided. [L0988.015]
- When researching a product, if nearly every recommendation, review or guide names the same single brand, treat the niche as brand-dominated. Consumers pointed to one brand first show high brand loyalty. [L0988.017]

**Personal judgement**

- Test your niche by instant brand association. If the first brands that come to mind are specific company names, the niche has high brand loyalty and should be avoided. If you instinctively think of the product type rather than one or two brands, the niche has low brand loyalty and is acceptable. [L0021.008]
- Your own experience as a buyer can reveal which brands dominate a category, so it is a reasonable starting point for removing obvious brand-driven niches. Products you have not bought yourself still need a proper brand loyalty check before a final decision. [L0988.018]
- Intuition is the first check: if no brand comes to mind when you would buy a product yourself, that suggests no brand loyalty. Google Shopping data should then confirm or correct this impression. [L0455.007]
- A brand you recognize only because you bought from it yourself is not evidence that the wider market knows it. Treat recognition from your own purchases with caution. [L0455.008]
- A niche where intuition and search data both show no dominant brand is a stronger candidate. Such niches leave room for new stores, because consumers do not default to one brand. [L0455.014]

### Brand loyalty: categories to avoid

- Avoid niches with high brand loyalty: tablets (Apple, Samsung), headphones (Sony, Bose), digital cameras, gaming consoles, laptops and speaker systems. These meet other selection criteria but fail the brand loyalty test. [L0021.003]
- Avoid televisions. TV buyers research picture quality, warranties and reviews, then purchase the brand they trust. Manufacturers grant big-box retailers exclusive terms and pricing that a dropshipper cannot obtain. [L0022.002]
- Avoid tablets, televisions, laptops, video games, cameras and headphones, because customers already have predetermined brand preferences in these categories. [L0319.001]
- In the tablet market, most buyers choose iPad, followed by Microsoft Surface, then Android devices. Brand loyalty is set by manufacturer marketing before the purchase search begins. [L0319.003]
- Headphones priced at $200 and above are dominated by Bose, Beats, Sony and V-Moda. Customers in this range already have a brand preference due to manufacturer investment in brand building. [L0319.004]
- Video game console buyers choose between Xbox and PlayStation. No third option has viable market share because brand loyalty in gaming consoles is absolute. [L0319.005]
- A shopper who needs a tablet will most likely buy an iPad or a Samsung. A shopper who wants good noise-cancelling headphones will most likely buy Sony or Bose. Both niches are dominated by a few manufacturers and are not suitable for a new store. [L0988.007]
- Three-dimensional printers are dominated by Bambu Lab with strong brand loyalty. Remove them from the active list or move them to the bottom. [L0021.009]
- 3D printers are a high-brand-loyalty niche because the market is dominated by Bambu Lab. Buyers researching 3D printers are often pointed to this one brand first. [L0988.010]
- Treadmills from around 20 brands with roughly 100 products between them can offer enough variety, but buyers may still prefer the dominant brands. (2021, older) [L0968.092]
- A niche controlled by a few well-known brands, or one that is seasonal or saturated, is a weak choice. The niche needs enough variety in products and brands for buyers to choose a non-dominant brand. (2021, older) [L0968.089]
- A niche with few brands or too few products to sell online is weak, even when the product is heavy or large. Ask whether a supplier's niche gives enough variety. (2021, older) [L0962.094]

### Brand loyalty: categories that pass

- Persian rugs show low brand loyalty. Customers care about quality and style, not the manufacturer, so the niche is acceptable even though rugs are sold in big-box stores. [L0021.005]
- Stand-up paddle boards have no dominant brand equivalent like Apple or Bose. Customers buy on appearance and price fit, with no requirement for brand loyalty. [L0319.008]
- Stand-up paddle boarding is a product niche with low brand loyalty and a good fit for a niche list. Its buyers ask for the product itself, not a specific manufacturer. [L0988.008]
- Chandeliers are expensive products without brand loyalty that appeal to upper-middle-class customers. Numerous variations in style, size, color and light count make them suitable for online dropshipping. [L0319.009]
- Entryway chandeliers work well online because customers search by specific style and dimensions rather than manufacturer. A homeowner who cannot find a preferred 30" x 30" design locally will buy online when they find an exact match, regardless of brand. Upper-middle-class homeowners renovating create sustained demand. [L0022.005]
- Wall lighting fixtures are an effective niche and a strong cross-sell product for chandelier stores, because customers do not require specific brands. [L0319.010]
- Table lamps sell well because customers seek appearance and design, not brand identity. [L0319.011]
- Crown molding is suitable for dropshipping because it comes in many styles and designs. Customers choose on aesthetic fit, not brand. [L0319.012]
- Wallpaper is brand-generic. Customers buy multiple rolls for whole houses, generating multi-thousand-dollar orders, because style and pattern, not manufacturer, drive the purchase. [L0319.013]
- Interior designers are a key buyer segment in wallpaper-type niches. They buy for clients and search for exact pattern, color and texture names. Products that match these specific searches can attract buyers who would not find them at large retailers. [L1125.017]
- Mirrors and decorative vases sell effectively at appropriate price points. Customers do not prioritize brand when these products match their aesthetic vision. [L0319.014]
- Wooden flooring customers select by color, width and pattern. Brand identity does not influence the decision, which makes wooden flooring suitable for dropshipping. [L0319.015]
- Coffee tables, daybeds, fireplaces, chairs, shelving and other furniture items are suitable for dropshipping because customers do not require specific brands. [L0319.016]
- Low brand loyalty home and décor items with multiple manufacturers include stand-up paddle boards, chandeliers, wall lighting, table lamps, crown molding, wallpaper, coffee tables, sofas, fireplaces, mirrors, vases, bookshelves, dining tables and chairs, and wood flooring. Customers focus on style, function and price rather than brand. [L0021.007]
- Standup desks show wide manufacturer variation and are marked no for brand loyalty. [L0455.013]

### Brand loyalty test with Google Shopping

- Google Shopping is the data check for brand loyalty. Reach it by searching the niche keyword on google.com and opening the Shopping results. It shows which brands appear on the first results page. [L0455.003]

**Procedure: brand loyalty test for each niche**

1. Ask yourself whether any brand comes to mind immediately when you imagine buying a product in the niche. If none does, this points toward no. [L0455.004]
2. Copy the niche keyword, for example "chandelier", and search for it on google.com. [L0455.004]
3. Open the Shopping results. [L0455.004]
4. Review the brands shown on the first results page, including the brand list in the sidebar. [L0455.004]
5. Check the product names for manufacturer names. [L0455.004]
6. Decide: if the same few brand names keep repeating, mark yes; if many different and unfamiliar companies appear, mark no. [L0455.004]
7. If you marked yes, move the niche to the bottom of the list and continue researching the other niches. If you marked no, the niche can stay at the top as a candidate. [L0455.004]

- Judge the companies that manufacture the products, not the online stores that sell them. Ignore store names on Google Shopping when judging brand loyalty. [L0455.005]
- Do not confuse the retailer selling a product with the brand that makes it. Counting store names as brands gives a false picture of brand loyalty. [L0455.006]
- The sidebar on Google Shopping can list both retailers and brands. For standup desks, retailers such as Standup Desk Store, Vivo, Luxor, Simple Stuff and Costway appear alongside brands, so retailer names must be filtered out. [L0455.016]
- There is no fixed number of repeated brand names that defines brand loyalty on Google Shopping. The judgement rests on whether the first results page repeats the same brands or shows wide variation across many companies. [L0455.009]
- The brand loyalty column on the niche research worksheet takes only a yes or no answer. Mark yes when the same brands dominate the results and no when there is wide variation. [L0455.010]
- Switch Google Shopping from list view to grid view to scan many brand names quickly on the first results page. [L0455.018]

**Results from the brand check**

| Niche | What the first results page showed | Verdict and action | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tablets | Samsung about 7 times among roughly 19 listed results; Amazon and Apple about 4 times each; Lenovo 3 times; Microsoft once. A handful of repeated brands. | Yes, brand loyalty. Mark yes and move to the bottom. | L0455.011, L0455.017 |
| Chandeliers | Many different manufacturers: House of Hampton, Home Decorators Collection, Pottery Barn, Gallery Direct, Elencut Lighting, Warehouse of Tiffany, Pocini Euro Designs, French Empire, Maria Theresa, World Class Lighting, Luan18, Edvidi Pamina, Bella Chandelier and Everly Quinn Lustry. Only Pottery Barn was familiar. | No. The niche can stay at the top. | L0455.012, L0455.015 |
| Standup desks | Wide variation: Vivo, Luxor, Simple Stuff, Costway, Real Space, Seville, SHW, FlexiSpot, Walnut, Rosenbalt, Sabine and Vari among the brands, plus Uplift. | No. | L0455.013, L0455.016 |

### Retailers and big-box stores

- A product sold in big-box stores is acceptable for niche selection. A niche controlled by a few powerful brands is not. [L0021.006]
- Being sold in big-box stores does not disqualify a niche by itself. Persian rugs sold at Home Depot or Lowe's remain acceptable because buyers ask for the rug, not a brand. [L0988.006]
- Treating any product sold in big-box stores as a bad niche is a mistake. Look at whether buyers ask for a specific brand, not at where the product is sold. [L0988.014]
- Large retailers selling a product category do not disqualify it, because individual brands are often sold in only a few stores. (2019, older) [L1069.035]
- Niche validity is judged per product. A niche with many brands but few stores selling them is fine. If few advertisers are in Google Merchant Center or the free listings, that is an advantage. (2024) [L0856.044]
- Exclude a niche where big established retailers sell most of the brands. Focus on the brands those large retailers do not sell. (2020, older) [L0961.046]
- Avoid brands that are mainly sold by large retailers. Choose suppliers among the many makers of a product type rather than the few brands big retailers stock. (2021, older) [L0853.049]
- Local stores that stock only a few top brands do not rule out an online niche. If online-only retailers in the niche collectively list hundreds of brands that cannot be bought locally, there is enough variety to support online demand. (2021, older) [L0834.127]

**How the sources fit together**

- The 2019 units say big-box presence and large retailers do not disqualify a niche. The 2020 and 2021 units say to exclude a niche where big retailers sell most of the brands, and to avoid brands mainly stocked by large retailers. Apply the niche-level rule (big-box presence is acceptable) and the supplier-level rule (choose brands the large retailers do not carry). [L1069.035, L0357.013, L0961.046, L0853.049, L0021.006, L0988.006]

### Variety, competition and failed tests

- Before choosing a niche, verify it is not dominated by a few large brands. Tablet buyers go directly to Apple.com or Costco, so the market has little variety. Good niches have many products and brands, so customers search broadly within the category. (2021, older) [L0270.067]
- A niche where only big brands sell and no dropship-friendly competitors exist is a failed test. Niche up, sideways or pivot. (2023) [L0855.089]

### Validating how people buy

- Validate a niche by checking whether people buy out of pocket or through third parties. Hospital beds and mobility equipment are often purchased through insurance companies, which reduces profitability. Ask suppliers or competitors to understand actual purchase behavior. (2021, older) [L0270.070]
- Medical and mobility items such as stairlifts, lift chairs, CPAP machines and mobility scooters are often bought by older adults or caregivers. Health or medical claims in ads may face platform or regulatory limits in some markets. [L0546.010]

### Consumer and business buyers

- Research B2B niches the same way as B2C: check competitor traffic, Google Shopping competition and monthly search volume. Buyers still search and buy online, even if product names return few results. (2024) [L0971.012]
- Whether a niche has business buyers should not be a factor in niche selection. Consumer-only and mixed markets can both be profitable, so judge a niche on its other criteria. (2025) [L0972.095]
- The upper middle class label does not apply to business buyers, who are used to spending money. (2018, older) [L1109.018]
- Business buyers should not be ruled out by the demographic label; the 2025 approach judges by other criteria, while the 2018 label is a service-level description only. [L0972.095, L1109.018]

### Repeat purchases and cross-sell

- Repeat purchases are rare in most niches, and most traffic comes from first-time visitors. Use upsells, cross-sells, referral discounts for family and friends, and affiliate content for indirectly related products to get additional value. (2023) [L1283.068]
- Wall lighting is a strong cross-sell for chandelier stores. [L0319.010]

### Audience segments beyond income (Source C)

- Track buyer demographics in the sales data of winning products. In the example, the winning products mostly sold to women aged 45 and older, which helps refine audiences. [L1131.042]
- Find the customer segment that converts best in your past stores and write the research brief around its needs. In one tested case, the best audience was women over 45, so every product search was framed around their needs. [L1358.005]
- A dropshipping owner who has tested products, niches and countries over several years may find that one audience clearly outperforms the others, such as women over 45 in one documented case. Product research can then be filtered to that audience's needs, which gives a team member a precise target. [L1360.025]
- Women over 35 were the most profitable audience for fashion, jewelry, home decor and fitness items, while products aimed at men performed worse. Test this audience first when researching products for Germany and Australia. [L1431.007]
- Some sellers found that men aged roughly 35 and above were the easiest customers, generating few support emails, while women over 45 were another reliable group. The choice depends on which audience your own sales data shows. [L1432.017]
- If a product has two different buyer groups, such as partners buying gifts and parents buying for children, reach each group through creators whose followers belong to that group. Look at the followers of creators who already post content with that buyer type. [L1379.058]
- For Valentine's Day, focusing only on women as buyers is a common error. Men and parents also buy gifts on that day. [L1469.024]
- A jewelry store offered only one product at a time to organic traffic. About 30 percent of its viewers turned out to be men, so men's products were added to the store and purchases from men increased. [L1469.029]
- A product can be repositioned by changing who buys it. A product first aimed at women was marketed to men as a gift, and that switch in buyer and angle opened new demand. Test different buyer groups with the same product before dropping it. [L0552.057]
- A food vacuum sealer is more likely to sell to people storing dry goods in bulk, such as nuts, oats or coffee beans, than to daily cooks who can use jars. Target the bulk-storage buyer and check whether these buyers would need several units. [L1186.044]
- A product with a niche audience, such as alcohol-related items, can be limiting and may need a broader angle or a different target group to scale. [L0656.014]
- A product tied to a cultural or national identity, such as a map necklace of a home region, can reach a large audience of people who feel connected to it. Target that diaspora in several Western countries such as the US, UK and France. Offer a second item the buyer chooses for their home country as a free gift to raise the perceived value of the order. [L0661.066]

**Prompt**

```
What is the demographic of buyers of [horse saddles]? Tell me where they are located, their average household income, their hobbies, the pages they follow and the magazines they read.
```

[L0667.049]

### Broad targeting and narrowing

- Start with broad interests and a broad audience. Narrow to the age, gender and interest that win once a winning audience, age, gender and interest are found, and do not niche down before a winner exists. [L0773.035, L0774.036]

### Enthusiast markets (Source B 2021-22, older)

- An enthusiast market is one where people buy because they want the products and enjoy them, not only because they need them. Enthusiast markets are easier and cheaper to market than need-based ones, such as fridges, which the lesson treats as not enthusiast. (2021-22, older) [L0458.028]
- A niche is an enthusiast market when buyers want the products for a hobby or recreation rather than need them. Products people buy to create things always count as enthusiast. (2021-22, older) [L0490.009]
- Survival and off-grid gear is classed as a want, not a need, because buyers can still live on the grid. For this reason it counts as an enthusiast market. (2021-22, older) [L0490.010]
- Target an enthusiast market: customers who buy products for a hobby, passion or activity they choose, not something they must do daily. Examples include surfboards, stand-up paddle boards and kiteboarding gear. (2021-22, older) [L0994.007]
- Enthusiast buyers usually have more disposable income and want the product, so a high price is less of a barrier. They also haggle less, which makes customer service and marketing easier. (2021-22, older) [L0994.008]
- Fitness equipment such as exercise bikes and cardio machines is a good fit: enthusiasts recognize several brands from gyms and fitness media, while outsiders do not. If you already recognize every brand in a niche without researching it, the niche is probably too mainstream. (2021-22, older) [L0994.016]

#### Further details

- If uncertain whether a niche has high or low brand loyalty, do not delete it yet. Module 2 software automatically analyzes brand loyalty for all niches and identifies which ones fail this test. [L0021.010]

- Launch your niche research worksheet. Survey your niche list and note which products instantly call to mind specific brand names. Demote or remove niches that are plainly dominated by one or two major brands. Retain niches where dominance is unclear-they're candidates for Module 2 testing. Finalize and check off your list. [L0021.011]

- Remove niches where a few big brands dominate and shoppers pick a specific brand by default, such as tablets, headphones, digital cameras, gaming consoles, laptops and speaker systems. These niches usually pass other product filters but fail the brand loyalty test. [L0988.001]

- 1. Open your niche research list. 2. Read through every niche and look for those that are obviously dominated by a few big brands. 3. Remove only the niches where you know a few brands dominate the market. 4. Leave niches you are unsure about on the list, without deleting them. 5. Mark this lesson step as complete and move on to the next task. [L0988.011]

- Do not delete a niche when you are unsure whether brand loyalty is high. Keep uncertain niches on the list and check them later with a brand-loyalty test in the research process, which will show whether the niche has brand loyalty. [L0988.012]

- Deleting niches you are not sure about wastes good options early on. Only remove niches that are clearly dominated by a few brands, and let a later check decide the rest. [L0988.013]

## Demand, Seasonality and Evergreen Testing

### Two tests before time is spent on a niche

- Validate every niche with at least two tests before investing time: demand (minimum 10,000 average monthly Google searches) and seasonality (evergreen check). Drop niches that fail either test early. [L0451.001]
- The Demand Test checks that people actually want the products in a potential niche. A pass validates real market demand. [L0047.001]
- The Evergreen Test decides whether a niche is seasonal or evergreen, meaning it has year-round demand. [L0047.003]
- Run the evergreen test on each niche to confirm steady demand across the year, not peaks at certain times. [L1057.004]
- Before committing time to a niche, verify that enough buyers exist, using market research. [L0769.019]
- Avoid seasonal niches for the first store. Profit is concentrated in a small time window, which lowers viability. [L0047.004, L0855.087 (2023), L1002.012 (older, 2019)]
- Market research matters most for long-term product survival, so judge a product on sustained demand trends, not on a short spike in ads or searches. [L0636.018]

### Demand threshold: the 10,000-search minimum

- The minimum is 10,000 average monthly Google searches per niche, measured as a consistent monthly average over months. [L0451.002, L0451.012]
- At or above 10,000 in the country where you sell is a green light to continue. [L1072.004]
- Mark any niche below 10,000 in red and deprioritize it. [L0045.005]
- Read the number against the threshold only. Do not compare it with other niches' volumes. A similar monthly range for different niches is expected. [L0451.006]
- The threshold is one criterion among many, not a standalone winner marker. Viability comes from combining all research criteria. [L0971.072]
- In 2024 a core keyword at about 10,000 monthly searches was still the working threshold for a viable niche. It is always judged together with competition, Google Shopping results and other research data. No fixed 500,000-search requirement applies. [L0971.083 (2024)]
- The demand figure is the average monthly searches for the niche keyword reported by the research tool. [L1081.010]
- The minimum is also reported as "about 10,000 per month" in a 2022 lesson. [L0969.020 (older, 2022)]
- A 2023 lesson applies the same 10,000 figure to the niche keyword and the average across the niche, and says to use it together with the other research tests, not on its own. [L0934.023 (2023), L0835.007 (2023)]
- A 2018 lesson set the same minimum for the UK and the US, measured as search volume, not clicks. [L1085.019 (older, 2018)]
- Above 10,000, no specific higher or lower number has proven to predict better store success. [L0666.004 (2024)]
- Search volume above 10,000 does not reliably indicate higher or lower success or competition. Volume alone is not a ranking signal. Judge success over time, after the store is live, optimized, and has more suppliers and customer data. [L0666.005 (2024)]
- A niche above 1 million searches has no upper limit. Narrowing it to a sub-niche is optional and only makes sense if it sharpens the store's focus. [L0663.074 (older, 2019)]
- Average monthly volume reflects general interest in a niche, not the traffic you will get. Actual traffic comes from brand, supplier and SKU keywords, so conversion math based on niche volume is not useful for forecasting. [L0803.015 (2022)]
- A 2018 lesson also checks that the average product price is $200 or more alongside 10K Google searches and evergreen demand. [L1109.016 (older, 2018)]

#### Thresholds by market (sources differ; each applies to a different test)

| Market / measure | Minimum | What it applies to | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Any target country, niche keyword (demand test) | 10,000 average monthly searches in the country where you sell | Demand test for a niche | L1072.004, L1072.013, L1085.019 (older, 2018) |
| US and Canada targeted together | 90,500 US searches is sufficient even if Canada shows 8,100 | Combined two-country targeting | L0268.001 (older, 2020) |
| Small-population countries, e.g. New Zealand | Niche up until the niche reaches about 10,000 | Demand test in a small market | L0806.003 (2024) |
| US, main keyword for a product type | 10,000 | Main keyword check (Source B) | L0458.026 (older, 2021-22) |
| Australia or smaller country, main keyword | 5,000 | Main keyword check (Source B) | L0458.026 (older, 2021-22) |
| US, combined niche total | 50,000 | Traffic volume (Source B) | L1485.007 (older, 2021-22) |
| Australia and other countries, combined niche total | 20,000 | Traffic volume (Source B) | L1485.007 (older, 2021-22) |

- The sources disagree. The 10,000 figure of the demand test (Source A) and the 10,000 / 5,000 figures for a main keyword (Source B, 2021-22) apply to one keyword check. The 50,000 / 20,000 figures apply to the combined total of all relevant product keywords in a niche, used as the traffic test. [L0458.026, L1485.007, L1485.008]
- The 10,000 minimum stays the same for every country. A smaller market gets no lower threshold. A product that falls short there needs a broader or combined niche to reach 10,000 in that market. [L1072.013]
- Population size does not change how you test demand. Judge a product by its search volume in the target country, not by how many people live there. [L1072.001]
- Do not decide that a small country cannot support a product because its population is small. Use the search-volume test for that country. [L1072.010]
- Do not compare a smaller country's volume with US numbers and reject it for being lower. The target country's own volume is the only one that matters. [L1072.011]
- A niche that fails the 10,000 minimum in a smaller country does not mean you change your research method. You need a niche in that country that reaches 10,000. [L1072.006]
- Example: stand-up desks had 6,600 searches in the UK (fail) and 40,000 in the US (pass). [L1072.005]
- Example: stand-up paddleboards showed about 40,500 average monthly US searches in 2020, used as a volume check when comparing product keywords. [L1111.188 (older, 2020)]

### Demand test procedure in research tools

Procedure, the source's own site (demand test for a target country). [L1072.002]

1. Open the keyword research tool at the source's own site
2. Select the target country.
3. Search the product keyword, such as "stand-up desk".
4. Read the search volume shown for that country.
5. If the volume is 10,000 or more, the niche passes and you can move forward.
6. If the volume is below 10,000, niche up to a broader category and test again.
7. If it is still below 10,000, test an alternative niche.
8. Only if no single niche reaches 10,000, combine two similar niches so their combined search volume reaches 10,000.

Procedure, Source A research tool (niche test). [L0451.005]

1. Copy the niche name from the niche research worksheet.
2. Open the research tool, set the country dropdown to the selling country (default US), paste the niche and click Search.
3. Read the monthly search volume. If it is at least 10,000, the demand test passes (green box). If not, the box is red and the text says the niche fails.
4. Copy the monthly search number into the worksheet's demand column.
5. Read the evergreen result. A green box with the message that the niche shows little to no seasonality means it passes. A seasonal result means it fails.
6. Copy the average price from the price analysis at the bottom of the tool into the worksheet's average price column, rounded as shown.
7. Mark the seasonality column yes or no accordingly.
8. Refresh the page before testing the next niche.

- Set the country dropdown to the country where you plan to sell, not where you are located. The default is US. [L0451.004]
- In the research tool, a passing niche shows a green result box with a message that it passes. A failing niche shows a red box, and the text names the failed test, either demand or evergreen (seasonality). [L0451.016, L1075.005]
- The tool analyzes the search-volume graph itself and reports seasonality automatically, so you do not need to read the graph manually to judge seasonality. [L1075.003]
- Example: a wine refrigerator niche showed over 14,800 monthly searches, passed the demand test, got a green evergreen box for little to no seasonality, and passed the price analysis. [L1075.004]
- Example: a Christmas tree stand niche passed demand but failed the evergreen test for strong seasonality. Its average price of $43.15 also failed the price analysis. The tool shows the reason in the text box next to the result. [L1075.006]

### Keyword tools and their limits

#### Country and setup rules

- Select the target country before running a search. Changing the country after a search still shows the earlier country's data. [L0247.010 (older, 2021)]
- Select the country first when checking whether a tool returns real results. Zero results in an otherwise working account can signal a glitch worth reporting to support. [L0853.085 (older, 2021)]
- The same keyword has different volumes in different countries, so select the target country before searching. [L1072.003]
- A tool's keyword data for a brand-new Google Ads account gives very broad search volume ranges. The data becomes more accurate once the account starts spending money. [L1277.020 (older, 2020)]
- Check whether a keyword has an accurate figure before you rely on it. The rank of a demand-tool result should fall between 1 and 1,000,000. A reading above 2,000,000 is not expected and should be double-checked before use. [L0360.001 (2024)]
- Demand graphs built on low search volume become spiky and volatile, because they rely on few average searches. Spikes on low-volume keywords carry little signal. Check the search volume figure at the top of the tool before reading the trend line. [L0360.002 (2024)]
- A flat line at the start of a trend graph usually means search volume was too low to show, not that the niche is seasonal. [L0806.005 (2024)]

#### Tool limits (values differ by year; check the current plan)

| Tool | Limit as stated | Workaround or note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ubersuggest free, 2020 | 5 searches per day, then 24-hour wait | Chrome extension gives all searches without the daily limit | L0268.002, L0967.012, L0671.167 (older, 2020-21) |
| Ubersuggest free, 2020 (other figure) | 4 searches per day | Chrome extension gives unlimited daily searches | L1277.021 (older, 2020) |
| Ubersuggest free, 2021-22 lesson | 3 free daily searches | Free accounts have a daily limit | L0771.019 (older, 2021-22) |
| Ubersuggest 7-day trial | Full access to all searches for 7 days | Get the needed data, then cancel before the billing date | L0268.069, L0967.012 (older, 2020) |
| Ubersuggest Chrome extension | Unlimited searches within the browser | Free workaround for the daily limit | L0268.068, L1111.015 (older, 2020) |
| Google Keyword Planner | Broad ranges (10k-100k) rather than exact numbers | Requires a Google Ads account, and ads must be turned on at least once; slower setup than Uber Suggest | L0268.002, L0967.013 (older, 2020) |
| Keywords Everywhere | Free Chrome extension with search volume and related data | Useful where the program's tool is not available; some users reported problems in certain countries, so check against another source | L0270.005 (older, 2021), L0835.008 (2023) |
| Program's keyword tool (2021) | No search limit | Covers US, UK, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand and South Africa | L0671.027, L0671.166 (older, 2021) |
| Research tool, 2020 beta | No search limit; US and UK only | Gives average monthly searches, daily searches and related keywords; average monthly searches is the key figure | L1111.014 (older, 2020) |
| Keyword research tool, later | Unlimited searches for members | A free keyword tool can be used for demand checks | L0962.096 (older, 2021) |

- Free Ubersuggest usage can be used to check search volume before committing to a product. [L1111.015 (older, 2020)]
- A 2019 procedure for demand check on Google uses the same general method when a niche search is low. [L1002.008 (older, 2019)]
- Google Keyword Planner data gives a broad range in brand-new accounts. Check any tool's exact number against a second source before relying on it. [L1277.020 (older, 2020), L0835.008 (2023)]

#### Cost-per-click and competition figures

- Ignore CPC during niche research. Focus on long-tail product-level search volume instead. CPM varies by broader niche category and does not reflect your specific product opportunity. [L0272.008 (older, 2022)]
- For niche demand research, look at average monthly search volume for broad niche keywords to confirm people search for what you want to sell. Ignore the CPC for those broad terms, because ads run on product-level keywords that cost much less. [L0551.007 (older, 2020)]
- Ubersuggest can show average monthly searches for broad niche keywords. Use the volume and ignore the CPC shown for those broad terms. [L0551.077 (older, 2020)]
- CPC and competition figures from Google Keyword Planner or Ubersuggest refer to Google search text ads, not Google Shopping. Do not use them to set Shopping bids. [L0852.022 (older, 2020)]
- Measure demand by search volume, not impressions. If a product gets many impressions but few clicks, look up its search volume in Google Keyword Planner to see whether people search for it at all. [L1085.029 (older, 2018)]

### Keyword selection and search intent

#### Finding product keywords (procedure)

Procedure, finding specific product keywords from a broad category (Google). [L0251.031, L0251.056]

1. Go to Google.
2. Type your broad product category (e.g., "aquarium").
3. Review the autocomplete suggestions.
4. Note which suggestions are actual products and which are non-product searches (e.g., "aquariums near me").
5. Scroll to the bottom of the search results and review "Related searches".
6. Use the related suggestions Google provides (e.g., "aquarium tanks" instead of "aquarium") to identify specific product keywords that match your target customer's search intent.
7. Use specific product keywords instead of broad terms for your niche research.

- To find more rising keywords, use Google Keyword Planner. [L0636.015]
  1. Click "discover new keywords".
  2. Search a broad keyword related to your product, such as "dog leash" or "lights".
  3. In the results, click the "three months change" column to see which searches grew over the last three months.
  4. Use the results for product name ideas, SEO keywords and marketing angles.

Procedure, finding more search demand for a product with low volume (2019). [L1002.008 (older, 2019)]

1. Search the product term on google.com.
2. Scroll to the footer and note the "searches related to" terms.
3. Check the search volume of each related term, such as "kids ride-on cars", "push ride-on toys" or "ride-on toys".
4. If the combined demand is still under $10K, move one level up to a broader category (for example "kids rockers") and combine two niches to reach $10K.

#### Intent: buying terms, qualifiers and brands

- When checking keyword demand, pick keywords whose search intent is clearly to buy the product, such as "barbecue grills", not terms used for other purposes, such as "Korean barbecue restaurants". This step needs judgment, so the demand numbers alone are not enough. [L0965.015 (2024)]
- Example: the US term for a generic sauna showed about 165K monthly searches, but many are for gym or public saunas. Adding "home" dropped it to about 33,000, the number that matches home buyers. Keep or remove an adjective based on whether it changes buyer intent for the product you sell. [L1090.005 (older, 2021)]
- If a brand name gets more search volume than the niche keyword, the niche keyword probably has too many qualifiers. Remove qualifying words from the niche search and check the results again. Never use a brand name as the name of your store. [L0965.016 (2024)]
- Very broad keywords rarely convert, because shoppers searching them are often not ready to buy. Target specific buying keywords rather than broad category terms. [L1088.005 (older, 2020)]
- Buyers in brand-less niches search for product attributes such as a specific size, color and style. Those attribute searches create keywords you can appear for. Selling through a brand site or a comparison shopper still leads buyers to your store. [L0804.010 (2023)]
- Use 5 to 10 keywords for trend analysis: two or three direct product keywords plus related problem or niche keywords, since people search for the problem before the product. Compare alternative product names and keywords to choose the wording for copy and ad titles. [L0895.028 (Source C)]
- Compare product name variants in Google Trends and in a dropshipping research tool to see which term has more search volume. Then run the research with one chosen term. [L0970.022 (2023)]
- Broad keywords can inflate traffic estimates, because they mix uses that do not match your product. Searches for "winches" include boat and trailer uses, and keyword lists can include unrelated meanings such as a firearm brand or inch-to-metre conversions. Only count terms that match what you plan to sell. [L1485.011 (older, 2021-22)]
- Mark the traffic-volume question yes only if the main keyword meets the minimum for its market. [L0458.025 (older, 2021-22)]

#### Source B's keyword procedure (Ubersuggest, 2021-22)

Procedure, Ubersuggest keyword check for a market idea. [L1485.010 (older, 2021-22)]

1. Open the Keyword Ideas section.
2. Set the country dropdown to the market you will sell in, for example United States, United Kingdom, Australia or Canada.
3. Enter your market idea as a keyword, for example "4x4 accessories", and click Search.
4. Read the VOL column, which shows average monthly searches for that exact keyword in the selected country.
5. Review the similar keyword suggestions and add the relevant variations to your count.
6. If a broad term mixes several product types, search narrower terms such as "winches for trucks" and count those separately.
7. Ignore keywords with unrelated meanings and add up the relevant ones.
8. Enter the combined estimate in the market research tracker.

Procedure, Ubersuggest keyword check (older, 2021-22). [L0458.025 (older, 2021-22)]

1. Open a keyword tool such as Ubersuggest in your browser. The lesson says anyone can use it without signing up, though a CAPTCHA check may appear.
2. Set the country to your market, for example the United States.
3. Enter the main keyword for your product type and read its monthly search volume.
4. Check the variations shown, such as "for sale" or "for home" versions, and add them to your total.
5. Mark traffic volume as yes if the main keyword meets the minimum.

- Ubersuggest (ubersuggest.com) is a free keyword tool that shows monthly search volume for a term. Set the country before searching. [L0771.019 (older, 2021-22)]

### Combining related products and niching up

- If a niche is too narrow to pass the search-volume criteria, combine closely related product types, such as charcoal and gas barbecues, rather than unrelated ones. The charcoal barbecue example had about 6,500 monthly searches. [L0965.018 (2024)]
- Procedure, reaching 10,000 in the target country (research tool). If the volume is below 10,000, niche up; if still below, test an alternative; only if no single niche reaches 10,000, combine two similar niches. [L1072.002]
- Small-population countries: niche up (broaden the niche to a higher level) until it reaches the minimum. [L0806.003 (2024)]
- Very small sub-niches can still reach roughly 2 to 3 million people on Facebook, and about half may show buying intent. A small niche is worth testing if the pain point is clear and the ad shows it in the first few seconds. [L0638.026 (Source C)]
- A niche that feels small can still contain millions of people in the target audience, so even a small conversion rate from a narrow ad can indicate a viable market. [L1016.003 (Source E)]
- Niches can take off when one seller tests a product and others follow on TikTok and Facebook. Watch fast-growing sub-niches, such as golf in recent years, and track which products appear in new sub-niches to spot the trend early. [L0871.007 (Source C)]
- Niche accessories that are very expensive, such as premium phone cases, are unlikely to have enough monthly searches to be worth it. [L0855.090 (older, 2023)]
- If a product term stays near zero, search the broader niche or the problem, feeling or occasion the buyer has (e.g., "kids drawing", "gifts for Valentine's"). [L1183.013 (Source C)]
- Demand that follows the product, the problem and the wider market points to different levels of opportunity. Compare them in Google Trends. [L0708.050 (Source C)]
- A gift product can be promoted for two close occasions, such as Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, using the same product. Plan the creator content and ad angles for each occasion separately. [L1379.057 (Source C)]

### Recurring revenue and traffic volume

#### Recurring revenue (Source B, 2021-22)

- A market has recurring sales potential if the customer will buy several different product types over time, or if the main product has accessories or add-ons. A coffee machine can be followed by a grinder and mini roaster, and generators by log splitters and snow blowers. [L0458.023 (older, 2021-22)]
- Recurring revenue means one customer can buy several different product types from the niche over time. A durable item bought once and lasting for years gives little recurring revenue. [L0490.012 (older, 2021-22)]
- Repeat sales to the same customer carry no acquisition cost, so margins on the second and third sale are often higher. A niche that supports several products is worth more than a single high-ticket item. [L0458.024 (older, 2021-22)]
- Score every shortlisted market idea Yes or No for recurring revenue. Answer Yes only if the market offers several different products that would appeal to the same customer and could be sold to them over time. [L1485.003 (older, 2021-22)]
- Example: a 4x4 accessories niche scores Yes, because one buyer can later purchase rear cargo drawers, a nudge bar, a turbo system, then suspension or wheels, with email used to bring them back. A niche selling only expensive, long-lasting CNC machines scores No, because buyers rarely replace them and rarely buy a second unit of the same product. [L1485.004 (older, 2021-22)]

Procedure, checking recurring revenue when unsure. [L1485.005 (older, 2021-22)]

1. Open the competitor websites you already collected in competition research.
2. Check whether they sell a range of different products.
3. Check whether those products would appeal to the same customer.
4. If both are true, mark recurring revenue as Yes; otherwise mark it No.

- Recurring sales in other niches: games and entertainment (customers buy more games once bored with the first), subscription models (customers rebuy mop heads and replacement parts), and fashion (seasonal changes quarterly). [L0324.007 (Source C)]

#### Traffic volume

- Traffic volume is the combined monthly searches across the niche's products. The first example niche had at least 20,000 searches per month, which was far above the traffic targets in every country discussed. [L0490.015 (older, 2021-22)]
- Measure traffic volume as the number of people searching each month for the product types you plan to sell on the Google search network. Google is the main channel for a high-ticket dropshipping business, through paid ads or organic search. Bing is much smaller and not a significant part of the marketing effort. [L1485.006 (older, 2021-22)]
- Add up the monthly searches for all relevant product keywords as one combined total, not each keyword separately. The total must reach the country threshold to count as enough traffic. [L1485.008 (older, 2021-22)]
- Check that the market has enough online search traffic to support a business over the long term. Marketing mostly runs on Google, Google Ads and Facebook, so enough people must be searching for the product at any time. [L0994.017 (older, 2021-22)]
- Example, US keyword volumes (2021): about 450,000 monthly searches for "generator", about 74,000 for "generator for sale" and about 49,500 for "generator for home". For log splitters, "log splitter for sale" had about 12,000 monthly searches. Volumes of related products can be added to the niche total to show enough demand. [L0458.027, L0771.020 (older, 2021-22)]
- Thresholds for the combined total are shown in the market table above. [L1485.007 (older, 2021-22)]

### Google Trends: reading the five-year view

#### Setup

Procedure, checking seasonality in Google Trends (2025). [L1116.047]

1. Open trends.google.com.
2. Set the region to the country where the business operates.
3. Change the time range from past day to past 5 years.
4. Read the chart for yearly peaks and valleys, and compare the busy season with the off season.

- Check the demand trend over the past five years. [L0671.025, L0671.164 (older, 2021)]
- Do not use search trend data from around 2004 to judge a niche. Use the last five years, since search behavior has changed a lot. [L0671.026, L0671.165 (older, 2021)]
- Judge seasonality in Google Trends over five years for the target country, using the 0-100 scale. [L1090.006 (older, 2021)]
- Procedure, Google Trends check with the Source C method: search the exact product name, then the problem it solves, the solution it offers and several related keywords, and compare their interest over time. [L0708.050]
- Set the time range to the past 12 months and search the exact product keyword first. [L1183.024]
- Use the 12-month and 5-year windows on the product and related keywords. [L0895.021]
- In the Source A tool, change the time period from past day to past five years and set the country to the target market. The graph then shows week over week instead of month over month. [L0805.041, L0805.064 (2024)]
- Google Trends searched with the product term, the US set as country and five years of interest is the way to check whether people buy the product year-round. [L0357.004 (older, 2019)]
- Google Trends checks evergreen demand, meaning whether search interest holds over time. It does not show when people open emails or click ads. For ad click timing, use the day and hour breakdown in Google Ads reports. [L0971.082 (2024)]
- Procedure, checking a candidate's market trend. [L1174.032 (Source C)]
  1. Open Google Trends.
  2. Search the main product keyword or, if it returns little data, the niche or a closely related term.
  3. Confirm the term is trending or holding interest before moving the product forward.

#### Interpreting the readings

| Trend reading | Meaning | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Stays at 0 for 5-6 months | Not viable | L0636.014 |
| Upward trend | Strong sign | L0636.014 |
| Consistently between 25 and 75 | Evergreen niche; healthy trend | L0636.014, L0708.047, L0895.021 |
| Interest between 25 and 100 | Target range in the search procedure | L1183.013, L1183.024 |
| Stays in 25-75 for the next 2-3 months | Holds; check the graph over 12 months and 5 years | L0895.021 |
| 25 or below, or constantly at zero | Negative sign | L0895.021 |
| Never drops below 50 | Can sell year-round; seasonal peaks alone do not disqualify it | L1111.005 (older, 2020) |
| Score of 50 | Not a hard requirement; judge the depth of the dip and whether interest falls close to zero off-season | L1088.001 (older, 2020) |
| Dip to near zero every year for several months | Seasonal niche | L0671.025, L0671.164 (older, 2021) |
| Gradual decline | Acceptable | L0671.025, L0671.164 (older, 2021) |
| Collapse to near zero | Reason to avoid the niche | L0671.025, L0671.164 (older, 2021) |
| Peak-to-low drop of about 60% or more | Common warning sign for a first store | L0357.001 (older, 2019) |
| Dip repeats in the same period every year and lasts three months or more | Warning sign | L1279.015 (older, 2021) |
| Random swings, e.g. sales moving between 40 and 90 | Not a reason to reject a niche | L1279.015 (older, 2021) |
| Busy season more than double the off season | Consider a second store in an inverse-pattern niche sooner rather than later | L1116.049 (2025) |

- The Google Trends interest graph for a product should sit roughly between 25 and 75 to indicate a healthy trend. Also check whether the market is rising, steady or declining, using Google Trends and news. [L0708.047 (Source C)]
- Procedure, Google Trends check with a wider keyword. Look for interest over time between 25 and 100. A broad keyword flat at zero for one to two months is a red flag. [L1183.013 (Source C)]
- The 50 floor (Source A, 2020) and the 25 floor (Source C) are different judgments. Use 25 as the negative line and 50 as a strong year-round benchmark, not a hard requirement. [L1111.005, L1088.001 (older, 2020), L0895.021]
- Seasonality severity must match the benchmark shown in the course. Seasonality alone is not a disqualifier. [L0251.045 (older, 2023)]
- Example, with Google Trends interest that peaks around 75 and bottoms around 25, a store scaled to $100,000 in peak-month sales could still fall to roughly $33,000 in low months with no changes and perfect execution. At a 20% net margin, the store would earn about $20,000 in peak months and just over $6,000 in low months. [L0357.002 (older, 2019)]
- Read a trend graph carefully. Large recurring peaks mean the niche is cyclical, and a first store should avoid strongly seasonal niches. [L0806.005 (2024)]
- Google Trends seasonality score of 50 is not a hard requirement. Judge seasonal dips by depth and by whether interest falls close to zero in the off-season. [L1088.001 (older, 2020)]

#### Trend checks over time

- Check Google Trends across years rather than quarters to judge demand stability. Pick products that sell consistently, not trending items. Products that upper-middle-class buyers always need tend to hold up in a recession, while luxury items should be avoided. [L0804.014 (2023)]
- Demand is judged over a five-year window, not a snapshot. Check that a niche does not collapse. [L0671.025 (older, 2021)]
- Compare Google Trends and a dropshipping research tool to pick the term with more volume. Run the research with one chosen term. [L0970.022 (2023)]
- Trending products often return months later after a quiet period, so a product that went viral earlier is worth re-checking before you dismiss it. [L1186.001 (Source C)]

### Seasonal versus evergreen judgment

#### Rules for the first store

- For a first store, choose evergreen niches with steady sales week over week, month over month and year over year. Seasonal niches produce sales only in a few months and then collapse regardless of how well the store is run. [L0451.003]
- Do not start with seasonal niches as your first store. Slight seasonality (demand that does not drop to zero) is acceptable. Severe peaks and valleys complicate measurement of what actually works. [L0268.004 (older, 2020)]
- Seasonal products should not be the first store, because a season can pass before you know whether the store works. Test that the product sells year-round with an evergreen check before committing. [L1002.012 (older, 2019)]
- Seasonal niches with a deep off-season are poor choices for a first store. Demand swings, operations are hard to standardize, and geo-targeting may be needed. Consider them for a second or third store, after a first store is stable year-round. [L1113.007 (older, 2022)]
- If a niche is seasonal, a first store should avoid it. [L0855.087 (older, 2023)]
- A niche with a seasonal peak is acceptable only if the valleys between peaks are not too low. Seasonal niches are generally not recommended. [L0834.008 (older, 2021)]
- For a first store, avoid niches with strong seasonal swings. A niche that never falls close to zero is still seasonal but less risky. [L0357.001 (older, 2019)]
- Outdoor patio furniture shows a strong seasonal dip, so it is better kept for a second or later store rather than the first. [L0967.010 (older, 2020)]
- A seasonal store launched during its low season still produces some sales and experience. Finish setup, keep suppliers engaged and prepare for the next peak instead of restarting the niche search. Plan a non-seasonal second store or a product that covers the off months. [L1285.010 (2024)]

#### Acceptable seasonality

- Seasonality is acceptable if demand remains consistent year-round with only minor fluctuations. Use Google Trends (five-year view) to verify, watching for drops that do not approach zero. [L0268.006 (older, 2020)]
- Seasonal dips do not automatically disqualify a niche. A niche that dips in Q4 but grows year over year can beat a steady niche with much lower search volume. Weigh all research factors together. [L0934.024 (2023)]
- Seasonal niches are acceptable if Google Trends seasonality severity matches the benchmark in the course. [L0251.045 (older, 2023)]
- Mild seasonal peaks, such as a November rise from gift buying, are not a reason to add other niches. Launch with the niche as it is. Extreme seasonality, where sales nearly vanish for most of the year, is a poor fit. [L1116.048 (2025)]
- Holiday sales spikes in inherently non-seasonal niches are normal and acceptable. For example, paddleboards sell more in summer. Seasonal products such as holiday decorations are not acceptable in a general niche. [L0272.009 (older, 2022)]
- A niche is not seasonal if some products sell in fall and winter while others sell in spring and summer. Together they can produce steady revenue year-round. [L0854.101 (older, 2022)]
- Do not choose niches where all seasonal items dominate unless demand is proven to be high and remains elevated year-round. [L0249.006 (older, 2022)]
- A bump that only lifts Q4 for a few weeks is holiday demand. A product that sells all year is not seasonal. A product is seasonal only if demand falls to a clear low for most of the year. [L1090.006 (older, 2021)]

#### Identifying the pattern

- To check seasonality, compare the average monthly search volume with the trend chart. If most of the yearly search volume falls in November and December, the product is seasonal. [L0970.018 (2023)]
- Example: a keyword averaging 30,000 searches per month, with about 270,000 of the yearly total in November and December, shows a clear seasonal peak. Such a product is seasonal even if it sells steadily the rest of the year. [L0970.019 (2023)]
- A niche passes the seasonality test only with 4 out of 4 seasons, meaning it sells month over month and year over year, so it can sell year-round. [L1081.009]
- Check seasonality with a trend graph. Strong peaks and valleys indicate a seasonal product, while a flat line indicates an evergreen product. [L1285.009 (2024)]
- Use the US Census Bureau's quarterly retail e-commerce sales data at census.gov to check seasonality. Look at the unadjusted series, where Q4 shows the largest peak in most years. [L1285.100 (2024)]
- Seasonality matters for Google Trends in a 2019 lesson: seasonal dips should be checked against whether the product sells year-round. [L1002.012 (older, 2019)]
- A seasonal product shows a repeated rise in a regular period such as September to November before winter. When the last year shows a stronger spike than prior years, it suggests higher potential for the coming year. [L0895.022 (Source C)]

#### Using the seasonal result

- If the busy season is more than double the off season in Google Trends, consider building a second store in a niche with the inverse pattern sooner rather than later. [L1116.049 (2025)]
- Test products with a gift angle only for a season, since a Christmas-driven product can sell well in one quarter and then fall off. Look for problem-solving products with viral potential for long-term runs. [L1440.007 (Source C)]

### Evergreen categories and product choice

- If starting directly with private labeling without dropshipping proof, choose forever-green niches (selling year-round) rather than trend products that peak and then die within months. This reduces loss risk on inventory investment. [L0324.005 (Source C)]
- Forever-green categories include seasonal fashion (jewelry, apparel renewed each season), home health products (posture correctors, foot correctors, leg supports), home improvement, kitchen utilities and appliances. [L0324.006 (Source C)]
- Prefer evergreen products that sell all year over niches that work only for one to three months. Finding a product that earns 10,000 to 30,000 per month is hard, and replacing products every few months is costly. Look for products that solve everyday problems, since many sell year-round. [L0694.009 (Source C)]
- Prefer products that can run all year rather than seasonal or one-event products, unless the seller deliberately chooses a season. [L1177.003 (Source C)]
- Evergreen products that sell in all four seasons should be sourced first. Seasonal items are added later. [L0472.059 (2025)]
- Evergreen products that people keep buying over years are preferred, even if demand dips for a while. Luxury items can still be evergreen, and a short-term slowdown in purchasing frequency is not a reason to abandon a niche. [L0967.008 (older, 2020)]
- Prefer evergreen niches that sold well in the past and will sell in the future over products that are only trending. Long-term demand is what makes a store a lasting asset. [L1069.033 (older, 2019)]
- Pet toys keep selling consistently and are a reasonable candidate for testing. Evergreen categories like this carry lower trend risk than short-lived viral products. [L1172.012 (Source C)]
- Women's fashion is an evergreen category that performs well across seasons. If a product underperforms in one country, test it in another market before dropping it. [L1173.007 (Source C)]
- Seasonality and fast-growing niches create windows of opportunity. Pet products and winter-season items showed strong momentum in the period described. [L0708.018 (Source C)]

### Trend timing and short-lived products

- A 90-day revenue trend should be checked before committing to a product. A product that peaked and is now slowing needs a different approach or should be skipped. Adjust the plan on the trend, not only on the last 30 days. [L1187.016 (Source D 2026)]
- Product demand can drop after a short seasonal peak. A portable blender that sold well for a period stopped selling. Check the recent sales trend before putting money into ads and prepare a replacement product in advance. [L1184.069 (Source C)]
- Procedure, checking a trend before stocking merchandise. [L1214.028 (Source C)]
  1. Search the keyword and view the trend graph, both worldwide and over the past five years.
  2. Judge whether interest is rising, steady or falling, and where you are on the curve.
  3. Estimate how long the trend will last, for example until a season or league ends.
  4. Launch while interest is rising or near its peak, not after it has passed.
  5. Avoid buying large stock at the end of a trend.
- Buying bulk team merchandise tied to a match or season result can leave unsold stock and chargebacks if the team does poorly. Buyers feel misled when the product no longer fits the outcome they expected. [L1214.029 (Source C)]
- A product that went viral earlier can return, so check it again before dismissing it. [L1186.001 (Source C)]
- In 2020, gym and fitness equipment had stock shortages. Demand spiked when gyms closed and inventory had been planned for normal demand. Check inventory risk in niches with sudden demand spikes. [L1277.024 (older, 2020)]

### Seasonal stock, ad spend and budgets

- For a seasonal product, keep ad spend low or pause ads in the warm months, from April to October. Resume ads once the cold season returns. [L0492.011 (Source C)]
- Check whether your product sells on a seasonal pattern or year-round before planning budgets and campaigns. Knowing the buying seasons tells you when to increase spend and when to reduce it. [L1268.010 (Source D 2026)]
- Judge the store's margin across the year. If a store can reach a 20% net margin, it is better to have that margin all year than to rely on a seasonal niche with large swings. Seasonal niches are not automatically excluded, but the owner must decide whether the swings are acceptable. [L0357.003 (older, 2019)]
- A 20% net margin on the peak and low months of a seasonal niche (see the illustration above) shows the cash swing that the owner must accept. [L0357.002 (older, 2019)]

### Competitor and marketplace signals

- A category leader with a very large review count shows that demand for the product type is already proven. For example, a pet hair brush with about 138,000 Amazon ratings. Review volume on the top sellers is a quick sign of how big a niche is. [L0450.024 (Source C)]
- Evaluate demand by looking at the homepage of competitor stores, since products featured there are usually the best sellers. The Best Sellers tab on those sites shows which brands and suppliers make the top products. [L1069.036 (older, 2019)]
- There is no fixed number of reviews within the last 30 days that proves a product is selling. Use competitor homepages and best-seller sections as the signal instead. [L1069.037 (older, 2019)]
- Check inventory risk when a niche spikes suddenly, since stock planned for normal demand can run out. [L1277.024 (older, 2020)]

### Order of Research Checks

- Older advice (Source B, 2021-22). Run the traffic volume check after the recurring revenue check and before the final niche decision. [L1486.009]
- Complete the traffic volume check for all five shortlisted market ideas before making the final choice of niche. Traffic volume is the last research step before deciding which idea to build. [L1485.014]

### Recurring Revenue as the First Check

- Older advice (Source B, 2021-22). For each market idea, answer yes or no to recurring revenue potential. Answer yes only if the niche includes more than one product that the same customer could buy. The products must appeal to the same buyer. [L1486.004]
- Example of a yes: in a 4x4 accessories niche, a first sale could be rear cargo drawers, followed by a nudge bar, then a turbo system upgrade, then suspension or wheels, all sold to the same owner at different times. This makes the niche a yes for recurring revenue. [L1486.006]
- Example of a no: a niche selling only CNC machines is a no for recurring revenue. The machines are very expensive, last a long time, and are rarely replaced, so a second or third sale of the same product is unlikely. [L1486.007]
- To check recurring revenue potential for a market idea:
  1. Go back to the competitor sites from the earlier competition research.
  2. Check whether they sell a range of different products, and whether those products would appeal to the same customer.
  3. If they do, the market idea has recurring revenue potential and gets a yes. [L1486.008]

### Traffic Volume Thresholds

- Older advice (Source B, 2021-22). Traffic volume is the monthly number of people searching Google for the types of products you want to sell. It is the second research question and is measured after the recurring revenue question is answered. [L1486.009]
- The target is a combined total across all product keywords in the niche:

| Market | Combined monthly Google searches (target) |
|---|---|
| United States | 50,000+ |
| Australia and any other country outside the US | 20,000+ |

  [L1486.011]
- Do not judge each product keyword on its own when checking the traffic target. The 50,000 or 20,000 figure is a combined total across all relevant products in the niche, so add up the volumes of every product keyword that fits. [L1486.012]
- For the shortlist decision, a rough estimate of monthly search volume is enough, because the goal is to see whether a market is large or small. Keyword tool volumes are approximations, so exact precision is not needed. [L1486.024]
- Once the summed volume of relevant keywords is clearly above the target, stop counting. Either enter the target figure itself (50,000 for the US, 20,000 for other countries) or enter the exact total, as long as the total is clearly above the target. [L1486.025]
- Example: a US total of roughly 200,000 monthly searches was entered as one number after clearly passing 50,000. Exact summing matters mainly when the total is close to the threshold. [L1485.020]

### Counting Keyword Volume with Ubersuggest

- Older advice (Source B, 2021-22). Ubersuggest requires a paid account for full search volume data. Use this procedure for every shortlisted market idea:
  1. Sign up for an Ubersuggest account to access full search volume data.
  2. Open the Keyword Ideas section of Ubersuggest.
  3. Review the market ideas on your research tracker and enter the main keyword for one idea, for example 4x4 accessories.
  4. Set the country in the country dropdown to the market you will sell in, such as English / United States, English / United Kingdom, English / Australia, English / Canada or Japanese / Japan.
  5. Click Search.
  6. Read the VOL column for the main keyword and hover over the volume to see the exact monthly searches.
  7. Go through the suggestion list and keep only keywords that match the products you would sell.
  8. Enter product-specific keywords, such as winches for trucks, to narrow results to the right product type.
  9. Check for regional wording, such as truck accessories in the US, and search those terms too.
  10. Add up the monthly volumes of all relevant keywords for the market idea.
  11. Enter the combined total in the Traffic Volume column of the research tracker.
  12. Repeat steps 3 to 11 for every shortlisted market idea. [L1486.015]

### Filtering Keywords

- Count a related keyword only if you could realistically sell that product. For example, winches for UTV could be counted, while winches for trailers should be excluded when the store sells truck accessories. Narrow broad terms with a qualifier such as for trucks to remove results that do not match your product. [L1485.021]
